I. OVERVIEW
[ 1 ] In August 2021, at the height of the Delta variant wave of the COVID-19 pandemic, the Government of Canada issued an announcement that all employees of federally regulated transportation companies would be required to be vaccinated against COVID-19 over the next two months, as a condition of their employment. Canadian National Railway Company (CN), the Respondent, advised its employees of this requirement. It instigated a process by which employees could apply to qualify for an exemption to the vaccine mandate on medical or religious grounds. Cory Perren, the Complainant, was an employee of CN at this time, as well as a lifelong Christian and follower of the Evangelical Free religion. He sought an exemption from the vaccine mandate from his employer on the basis that his religious conscience did not permit him to receive the vaccine.

[ 2 ] Based on a paper review of his application, CN denied Mr. Perren’s request for an exemption as it determined that he had failed to establish a link between his religion and his belief that he could not receive the vaccine. While Mr. Perren attempted to engage with his employer to understand its decision and to answer its questions, CN informed him that he could not grieve or appeal the decision. CN placed him on unpaid leave in early November of 2021, and, three months later, CN terminated his employment.

[ 3 ] Mr. Perren filed a human rights complaint against his former employer under section 7 of the Canadian Human Rights Act , R.S.C., 1985, c. H-6 (the “Act”), alleging that his termination was discriminatory on the ground of religion. This complaint is the subject of these proceedings.

II. DECISION
[ 4 ] For the reasons that follow, Mr. Perren’s complaint is substantiated. The scope of the freedom of religion is a complex and divisive issue that has challenged the judiciary. The 2004 Supreme Court decision in Syndicat Northcrest v. Amselem , 2004 SCC 47 [ Amselem ], which serves as the guiding post for the recognition of this right, was decided by a narrow majority of five judges. It is therefore unsurprising that, in the early stages of the COVID-19 pandemic when concerns for the health and safety of the Canadian population were still at their highest, employers, faced with determining how to respect this right while complying with the government’s vaccine mandate, found it challenging to do so. And yet, it is especially in these times of societal upheaval that we must be able to rely on the fundamental human rights principles that protect inherent personal characteristics from adverse treatment. For the devout, this includes their relationship with God.

[ 5 ] Mr. Perren discharged his onus of establishing that he holds a deep and sincere religious belief that prevented him from receiving the COVID-19 vaccine and complying with CN’s vaccine mandate. CN’s suspension and subsequent termination of his employment was based on his refusal to receive the vaccine on religious grounds and constitutes discrimination. Mr. Perren communicated sufficient information to CN for it to know that he required accommodation. Given CN’s failure to clarify its understanding of the nature of his religious belief and refusal to engage with him, it is responsible for its misunderstanding of Mr. Perren’s reference to his religious conscience. As a result, CN failed to provide a reasonable non-discriminatory explanation for the events.

III. ISSUES
[ 6 ] The issues in this case are:

1) Did CN discriminate against Mr. Perren in the context of employment, contrary to section 7 of the Act?

a) Did Mr. Perren have a characteristic protected from discrimination under the Act?

b) Did he communicate his religious belief to CN?

c) Did he experience an adverse impact? And

d) Was Mr. Perren’s religion a factor in the adverse impact he experienced?

2) Did CN harass Mr. Perren?

3) Did CN breach section 15 of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms (the “Charter”)?

4) What remedies, if any, are appropriate in the circumstances?

IV. CONTEXT
[ 7 ] Mr. Perren was an employee of CN from around December 13, 2010, until CN terminated his employment on February 11, 2022. He is a lifelong Christian and follower of the Evangelical Free religion.

[ 8 ] CN is a federally regulated employer, operating Canada’s largest railway with its transcontinental network spanning from Vancouver in the West to Halifax in the East and South through the United States of America to the Gulf of Mexico. The railway is an essential service and operated throughout the COVID-19 pandemic.

[ 9 ] In August 2021, Canada was in the fourth wave of the COVID-19 pandemic. The Government of Canada announced on August 13, 2021, that all employees of federally regulated transportation companies were required to be vaccinated against COVID-19 as a condition of their employment, originally by the end of October 2021. CN sent its employees a newsletter informing them of this announcement. Mr. Perren emailed his manager on the same day, referring to past conversations between them, reiterating that his religious convictions prevented him from receiving the COVID-19 vaccine.

[ 10 ] On October 19, 2021, the Government of Canada issued a Ministerial Order pursuant to section 32.01 of the Railway Safety Act , R.S.C., 1985, c. 32 (4th Supp.) (the “Order”) requiring all persons employed by CN to receive their first dose of a COVID-19 vaccine by November 15, 2021, and to be fully vaccinated against COVID-19 by January 24, 2022. Transport Canada also issued a document entitled “Guidance Material for Railway Companies” on how to implement the Ministerial Order (the “Guidance Material”).

[ 11 ] The Order set out limited exceptions to the vaccine mandate, including where an individual could not be vaccinated on the basis of a sincerely held religious belief. Employees were required to submit a sworn attestation regarding their sincerely held religious belief in the form specified by Transport Canada, which CN adopted and entitled “Request for Sincerely-Held Religious Accommodation Vaccination Requirement” (the “Request Form”). The Request Form required that an individual seeking this exemption describe the nature of their sincerely held religious belief or practice and the reasons why the religious belief prohibits them from receiving the COVID-19 vaccine.

[ 12 ] CN created a dedicated Religious Exemption Review Committee (the “Committee”) for the purpose of reviewing applications for religious exemptions from the COVID-19 vaccine mandate. It was comprised of senior members of CN’s leadership as well as a member of the Human Resources and Labour Relations team who provided administrative support and managed the inbox created to correspond with employees regarding their exemption requests.

[ 13 ] Mr. Perren wrote to Stephanie Hedley, the Director of Human Resources, on September 9, 2021, to ask how he could obtain a religious exemption from the vaccine mandate. He provided Ms. Hedley with a short statement describing the nature of his religious belief that prevented his vaccination by email and, further to her instructions, also completed the Request Form a few days later and returned it to the Committee.

[ 14 ] The members of the Committee each reviewed Mr. Perren’s application for religious exemption and then discussed it as a group. Applying the instruction provided in the Guidance Material, the Committee determined that Mr. Perren’s request did not satisfy the criteria. On October 8, 2021, the Committee advised Mr. Perren that it had denied his request for an exemption.

[ 15 ] Mr. Perren replied to the Committee, asking for greater clarity about the basis for its decision. The Committee informed him that its decision was final and that he was required to comply with CN’s vaccination policy.

[ 16 ] On October 29, 2021, Mr. Perren wrote to Ms. Hedley, relaying that he possessed prior email correspondence with his manager regarding his inability to get vaccinated. He asked Ms. Hedley for help in understanding the Committee’s decision. Ms. Hedley responded that there was no process in place for him to grieve its decision and that this was the final decision.

[ 17 ] On November 9, 2021, Mr. Perren reached out to his director explaining the situation and the religious basis for his request and asked him to intervene on his behalf with the Committee. This email was never received by the members of the Committee.

[ 18 ] Mr. Perren was placed on unpaid leave on November 17, 2021. CN sent Mr. Perren three letters between November 17, 2021, and January 27, 2022, while he was on leave advising him that employees were required to be vaccinated in order to return to work or would face termination.

[ 19 ] Mr. Perren’s employment was terminated on February 11, 2022.

V. LEGAL FRAMEWORK
A. Establishing a case of discrimination
[ 20 ] Mr. Perren alleges that CN engaged in a discriminatory practice in relation to his employment based on religion, contrary to section 7 of the Act. While Mr. Perren also raised section 10 of the Act, he made no submissions specific to this section, and I have therefore disregarded it when completing my analysis.

[ 21 ] Section 7 of the Act reads as follows:

7. It is a discriminatory practice, directly or indirectly,

( a ) to refuse to employ or continue to employ any individual, or

( b ) in the course of employment, to differentiate adversely in relation to an employee,

on a prohibited ground of discrimination.

[ 22 ] According to section 3 of the Act , religion is a prohibited ground of discrimination.

[ 23 ] To determine the existence of discrimination, the Tribunal engages in a two-step analysis. First, the complainant must establish a case of discrimination on a balance of probabilities. This is referred to as the prima facie (which is Latin for “at first face” or “at first appearance”) case of discrimination. In the 2012 decision Moore v. British Columbia , 2012 SCC 61 [ Moore ], the Supreme Court of Canada provided a breakdown of the elements that complainants must show as part of this first part of their case. Although Moore was decided on the ground of disability under the British Columbia Human Rights Code , this Tribunal has since adopted this test as the foundation for its analysis of alleged discrimination on a range of grounds pursuant to the Act.

[ 24 ] To establish discrimination, complainants are required to show that it is more likely than not:

A) that they have a characteristic protected from discrimination under the Act;

B) that they experienced an adverse impact; and

C) that the protected characteristic was a factor in the adverse impact.

[ 25 ] D iscrimination need only be one factor among other non-discriminatory factors for there to be a contravention of the Act: Quebec (Commission des droits de la personne et des droits de la jeunesse) v. Bombardier Inc. (Bombardier Aerospace Training Center) , 2015 SCC 39 [ Bombardier ] at paras 43–52.

[ 26 ] The respondent can present evidence to reasonably explain and refute the allegation of prima facie discrimination. The Tribunal will consider the evidence from parties on these allegations as a whole as it determines whether the complainant has discharged himself of his onus: Bombardier at para 58.

[ 27 ] If the complainant establishes a prima facie case of discrimination, the burden shifts to the respondent to justify their conduct within the framework of the exemptions available under human rights statutes: Moore at para 33. In the case of the Act, these exemptions are found at section 15, and a respondent must demonstrate, on a balance of probabilities, that it has accommodated those detrimentally affected to the point of undue hardship: Alberta Human Rights Commission v. Central Alberta Dairy Pool et al. , 1990 CanLII 76 (SCC) at 515. If the respondent fails to do so, discrimination will then be found to have occurred: McGill University Health Centre (Montreal General Hospital) v. Syndicat des employés de l’Hôpital général de Montréal , 2007 SCC 4 at para 50.

[ 28 ] In the case at hand, the Respondent’s evidence is centred on refuting the allegations of prima facie discrimination. It has not raised a justification under section 15 of the Act as part of its defence. The core of the debate between the parties and the evidence tendered is therefore limited to addressing the question of whether the Complainant has in fact succeeded in satisfying the Moore criteria.

B. Establishing the ground of religion
[ 29 ] In determining whether a complainant has established the existence of a protected characteristic under the Act, the Tribunal is looking to determine the existence of personal characteristics that are “immutable or constructively immutable”, changeable only at unacceptable cost to personal identity: Canada (A.G.) v. Johnstone , 2014 FCA 110 [ Johnstone ] at paras 68–70; see also Corbière v. Canada (Minister of Indian and Northern Affairs) , 1999 CanLII 687 (SCC) at para 13. Religious beliefs, although not immutable since individuals are free to change them, can be constructively immutable when deeply held or profound. Constructively immutable characteristics that are deeply held by an individual, such as religion or family status, are distinguished from decisions that amount to a personal choice, which human rights legislation does not protect (see, for example, Johnstone on family status). In cases involving religion, the law does not protect a personal secular choice: Amselem at para 39.

[ 30 ] The distinction between a deeply held constructively immutable religious belief and a personal choice is at the root of much of the case law on COVID-19 vaccine mandates, including in this case. It is also one of the key principles that help determine the existence of the ground of religion as established in Amselem , the leading authority for establishing the freedom of religion, and which both parties have relied on in this case. Decided under the Quebec Charter of Human Rights and Freedoms , the Supreme Court of Canada explicitly extended its analysis to the Charter (see Amselem at para 37). The principles the case establishes have also since been applied to the right to be free from discrimination under human rights legislation, including based on creed under the Ontario Human Rights Code, R.S.O. 1990, c. H.19 (see Clipperton-Boyer v. Redflagdeals.com , 2014 HRTO 1796 at para 16) and religion under the Act (see Bedirian v. Treasury Board (Department of Foreign Affairs, Trade and Development) , 2024 FPSLREB 58 at paras 27–32 ).

[ 31 ] In this case, the majority of the Supreme Court of Canada establishes the following two-part test, which an individual advancing an issue premised upon a freedom of religion claim must satisfy:

1. he or she has a practice or belief, having a nexus with religion, which calls for a particular line of conduct, either by being objectively or subjectively obligatory or customary, or by, in general, subjectively engendering a personal connection with the divine or with the subject or object of an individual’s spiritual faith, irrespective of whether a particular practice or belief is required by official religious dogma or is in conformity with the position of religious officials; and

2. he or she is sincere in his or her belief…

[ 32 ] Once a religious belief and its sincerity are established, freedom of religion is triggered.

[ 33 ] As part of its analysis, the Court provides several key guiding principles, which I summarize below. The Court’s two-part test, along with these principles, inform my analysis of the facts of this case.

(i) Religion is about a freely deeply held personal belief that tends to involve a connection with the divine

[ 34 ] The Court defines religion broadly: “Religion typically involving a particular and comprehensive system of faith and worship. Religion also tends to involve the belief in a divine, superhuman or controlling power”. In essence, religion is about

“freely and deeply held personal convictions or beliefs connected to an individual’s spiritual faith and integrally linked to one’s self-definition and spiritual fulfilment, the practices of which allow individuals to foster a connection with the divine or with the subject or object of that spiritual faith”

Amselem at para 39.

(ii) The right protects a profoundly personal and subjective conception, which does not require proving objective validity

[ 35 ] The emphasis is on the subjective aspect of the believer’s sincerity and the personal choice of religious beliefs. It is internally linked with an individual’s self-definition and fulfilment and is a function of personal autonomy and choice. The freedom of religion does not only protect those aspects of the belief or conduct that are objectively recognized by religious experts as being obligatory tenets or precepts of a particular religion: “… claimants seeking to invoke freedom of religion should not need to prove the objective validity of their beliefs in that their beliefs are objectively recognized as valid by other members of the same religion, nor is such an inquiry appropriate for courts to make”: Amselem at paras 42–43. The Court affirms that it is in no position to question the validity of a religious belief, notwithstanding that few share that belief, and that it is not its role to decide what any particular religion believes: Amselem at para 44, citing R. v. Jones , 1986 CanLII 32 (SCC), and Ross v. New Brunswick School District No. 15 , 1996 CanLII 237 (SCC).

(iii) There is a nexus with religion; secular, socially based or conscientiously held beliefs are not protected

[ 36 ] The practices and beliefs held must have a nexus with religion but must not be required by official religious dogma or in conformity with the position of religious officials: Amselem at para 46.

[ 37 ] The Court contrasts beliefs, conviction, and practices rooted in religion that are protected by the guarantee of freedom of religion, with those “that are secular, socially based or conscientiously held”: Amselem at para 39.

(iv) The believer’s personal sincerity drives the inquiry

[ 38 ] If anything, a person must show “‘sincerity of belief’ … and not that a particular belief is ‘valid’”: Amselem at para 43.

[ 39 ] Sincerity of belief simply implies an honesty of belief: Amselem at para 51.

[ 40 ] The Court’s role in assessing sincerity is intended only to ensure that an asserted religious belief is in good faith, neither fictitious nor capricious, and that it is not an artifice. Otherwise, nothing short of a religious inquisition would be required to decipher the innermost beliefs of human beings: Amselem at para 52.

[ 41 ] The sincerity of a belief is a question of fact and can be assessed using various non-exhaustive criteria, including the credibility of a complainant’s testimony and whether the alleged belief is consistent with their current religious practices. Since beliefs can change over time, the assessment of sincerity should not focus on past practice or belief but, instead, on a person’s belief at the time of the alleged interference with their religious freedom: Amselem at para 53.

VI. ANALYSIS
[ 42 ] Applying the test and principles from Amselem , I must first determine whether Mr. Perren had a personal characteristic protected from discrimination, as alleged in his complaint.

A. Does the Complainant have a characteristic protected from discrimination under the Act?
[ 43 ] To establish whether the Complainant has made out the existence of a prohibited ground in this case, I must examine whether he possesses a religious belief that is protected under the Act. Although CN accepts that Mr. Perren is a Christian, that fact alone does not satisfy the required threshold. The question I must determine is whether the protected ground of religion arises from the facts at issue. The issue is not whether Mr. Perren is a Christian or a follower of the Evangelical Free faith, but rather his belief that he cannot receive the COVID-19 vaccine. The question I must first answer is whether this belief is protected by the Act. In other words, and more specifically, did Mr. Perren hold a sincere, deeply held religious belief that prevented him from receiving the COVID-19 vaccine at the time of the events?

[ 44 ] The Respondent argues that the only evidence that the Tribunal should consider is the evidence that Mr. Perren submitted to the employer in the period leading up to his termination, rather than the additional evidence which he submitted over the course of the several days of hearing. I disagree. The Respondent relies on two decisions from the Nova Scotia Labour Arbitration Board in support of this view, neither of which are binding on me. In United Steel Paper and Forestry, Rubber, Manufacturing, Energy, Allied Industrial And Service Workers International Union, Local 5319 v Securitas Transport Aviation Security Ltd. , 2023 CanLII 91854 at para 57, the arbitrator relies on both the evidence that the grievor provided at the time of the events, as well as the evidence he introduced during the hearing, which does not support the Respondent’s argument. In Nova Scotia Union of Public & Private Employees, Local 13 v Halifax Regional Municipality , 2022 CanLII 129860, the arbitrator accepted that the relevant time to make the assessment of the exemption on the ground of freedom of religion was at the time of the events at issue. However, I am not an arbitrator sitting in review of the employer’s decision. Pursuant to section 50(1) of the Act, I am mandated to inquire into the complaint, which alleges discrimination.

[ 45 ] To determine whether discrimination occurred, I must be satisfied of the existence of a prohibited ground. If it is not established, then my analysis need not proceed further. If Mr. Perren demonstrates that he possessed a religious belief that prevented him from receiving the COVID-19 vaccine and, therefore, a protected characteristic under the Act, the question of whether the Respondent knew or ought to have known this when it terminated him for failing to get vaccinated becomes part of what I consider CN’s attempt to refute the allegation of prima facie discrimination ( Bombardier at para 64). For this reason, my analysis begins by examining all the evidence put forward by Mr. Perren in support that he possessed a sincerely held religious belief that prevented him from getting the COVID-19 vaccine at the time of the events.

[ 46 ] In addition to his own testimony, Mr. Perren called his father, Reverand Perren, a retired district superintendent and pastor of the Evangelical Free Church of Canada, as a witness. Mr. Perren initially sought to call his father as an expert in the teachings of the Evangelical church. In a ruling delivered on the bench, I found that Reverand Perren’s familial ties and relationship with his son created a conflicting interest that rendered him incapable of fulfilling the role of assisting me in an impartial, objective and independent manner, as is required of a properly qualified expert, the fourth criteria for admissibility established in R v Mohan, 1994 CanLII 80 (SCC) and White Burgess Langille Inman v Abbott and Haliburton Co. , 2015 SCC 23 (CanLII) . Reverand Perren was permitted to testify not as an expert, but as Mr. Perren’s father and former pastor, when Mr. Perren was growing up. His testimony largely focused on explaining the religious teachings he had imparted on his son.

1. Mr. Perren held a profound religious belief, involving a connection with the divine, that prevented him from receiving the COVID-19 vaccine
[ 47 ] Mr. Perren explained the nature of his belief as being composed of several parts.

[ 48 ] The first is that it is rooted in the belief that Jesus Christ resides in the body, which is a temple. He testified that “if we are created in the image of God, that is right down to our core, our DNA. Introducing something to that [the body] needs to be taken with a great care of caution and prayer”.

[ 49 ] The second is that where the Bible has no specific teaching on an issue he must decide, such as in the case of getting vaccinated, his faith dictates that his decisions are determined through the process of consulting with the Holy Spirit, who speaks to him through his conscience. As Mr. Perren stated: “Anytime that there is a decision that has to be made where we seek guidance to God the father and he uses the holy spirit and convicts us in whichever way he wants us to go to follow him”. Mr. Perren’s father testified that he taught Mr. Perren that, as Christ was preparing to leave, he promised his followers that he would not leave them alone in this world and would send the Holy Spirit who would then dwell in those who have come to have faith in Christ: “since this day, God the Holy Spirit dwells in those who put their faith in Christ and we can rely on him for our actions regarding the decisions we need to make”. Reverand Perren testified that Mr. Perren witnessed growing up that, when there were difficult decisions to be made and the scripture was not clear, they were called to spend time fasting and praying and that they would have “access to the heart and mind of God through sincere prayer”. He taught Mr. Perren that doing the right thing had to do with the “condition of your heart” and that it was important to “listen to your conscience because it is through your conscience that God the holy spirit will be speaking to you and giving you clarity on things”.

[ 50 ] Finally, Mr. Perren testified that, when the Holy Spirit speaks to him through his conscience, his faith dictates that he must test his conscience by praying, fasting, reading scripture, and by consulting with religious leaders. Once these tests have been applied and his conscience still has that conviction, he is not “released in that conviction”. Mr. Perren stated that, once convicted, it is clear that he is being spoken to directly by God through the Holy Spirit that this is what he is being told to do. For him not to do it would be directly disobeying God.

[ 51 ] Mr. Perren testified that the Holy Spirit came to him regarding the vaccine mandate, initially to his conscience. It was once he tested this conscience that he became convicted. He stated that he prayed about it, spent time in scripture, and spent time fasting. He testified that he felt “a deep deep conviction not to get vaccinated”, that he still feels this conviction, and that he truly believes that he was led by the Holy Spirit to follow God’s will that he should abstain from receiving it. Reverand Perren testified that he had had multiple conversations with his son about how he should proceed. It was obvious to him, he said, that Mr. Perren was “really struggling with this, didn't have peace in his heart, and that his conscience was troubled about this”. These observations support Mr. Perren’s testimony that he possessed a deeply held and profound belief.

[ 52 ] Mr. Perren described his decision not to get vaccinated as personal. He testified that his was “not a religion where I have to go to church twice per day, it is a personal relationship with Jesus Christ, that is what we are called to have and to pursue and I am still pursuing that”. While Reverand Perren also decided not to get vaccinated, he testified that other members of their religious community choose to do so and that this was accepted.

[ 53 ] Reverand Perren clarified that getting a vaccine was not a sin; it would only be considered a sin if one’s conscience dictated otherwise. He explained that this belief was grounded in scripture and that there was “a huge issue in Jesus’ day about eating meat that had been sacrificed to idols with believers feeling that they could not, in good conscience, eat it. Paul made it clear in the Romans that you should follow your conscience, and that those whose conscience freed them to eat it should eat and those whose it did not should not go against it”. Reverand Perren read into evidence Romans 14:14: “I am convinced, being fully persuaded in the Lord Jesus that nothing is unclean in itself. But if anyone regards something as unclean, then for that person it is unclean”.

[ 54 ] He also read into evidence Romans 14:21–23:

It is better not to eat meat or drink wine or to do anything else that will cause your brother or sister to fall. So whatever you believe about these things keep between yourself and God. Blessed is the one who does not condemn himself by what he approves. But whoever has doubts is condemned if they eat because their eating is not from faith and everything that does not come from faith is sin.

[ 55 ] I understood from Mr. Perren and his father’s testimony that, as a member of the Evangelical Free Church, Mr. Perren’s religious beliefs regarding vaccines do not dictate a specific outcome (i.e., to get or not to get vaccinated). Rather, his beliefs require that decisions involving putting unknown substances in his body be arrived to following an interaction with the divine through a religious process, from which he receives divine guidance on the path forward and which becomes a part of his relationship with God. In other words, the Evangelical Free Church’s beliefs possessed both an objective element, relating to adherence to a particular religious process, and a subjective conception, tied to each individual’s interaction with the divine and the conviction that flowed from this exchange. This personal and subjective conception of religion is precisely what I understand the Court in Amselem aimed to protect.

The meaning of the word "conscience"
[ 56 ] Contrary to what Ms. Hedley and Leslie-Ann Lewis, the two members of the Committee who testified, understood when reviewing Mr. Perren’s Request Form, it is clear to me that, when Mr. Perren wrote the following, his use of the word “conscience” was in no way secular:

I am a follower of Jesus and have spent many hours in prayer about this. After prayer, God has not afforded me a clear conscience with regards to taking this Vaccination. I must follow the path God leads me down as my faith is in him always.

And

I must follow Jesus and without having a clear conscience about taking the vaccination I cannot take it. I am requesting an exemption from the vaccination mandate. I must follow God in all he asks of me. Yet, my deep love for others makes me determined to seek alternatives that ensure others safety. I will look to the Company for recommendations for alternatives(sic) that comply with their vaccination mandate.

Rather, the “conscience” that Mr. Perren referred to was what he explained served as a conduit for the voice of the Holy Spirit, who came to him after prayer and communicated to him God’s message and will. In other words, conscience refers here to a religious conscience.

[ 57 ] The concept of conscience, as coming from God and tied to religion (and therefore distinct from a purely secular conscience), was discussed by the Supreme Court of Canada in R. v. Big M Drug Mart Ltd ., 1985 CanLII 69 (SCC) when the Court examined the purpose of protecting the freedom of conscience and religion pursuant to section 2(a) of the Charter. In examining the historical roots of the freedom, including the perception that the religious belief itself was not amenable to compulsion, Justice Dickson writes: “Attempts to compel belief or practice denied the reality of individual conscience and dishonoured the God that had planted it in His creatures . It is from these antecedents that the concepts of freedom of religion and freedom of conscience became associated, to form, as they do in s. 2(a) of our Charter, the single integrated concept of ‘freedom of conscience and religion’” (at 345) [Emphasis added]. Justice Dickson goes on to affirm that religious belief and practice are historically prototypical and, in many ways, emblematic of conscientiously held beliefs and manifestations (at 346–347).

[ 58 ] I distinguish this conscience, which, in the words of Iacobbuci J. in Amselem , is “rooted in religion” and which is what Mr. Perren described in his evidence, from a belief that is simply “conscientiously held ” and not protected by section 2(a) of the Charter: Amselem at para 39. I recognize that the wording of section 2(a) of the Charter refers to “freedom of conscience and religion”, as opposed to section 2 of the Act and section 15 of the Charter which both protect the ground of religion from discrimination, with no mention of the word “conscience”. However, I am not persuaded that I should draw any significance from this distinction given that the legislator refers in one case to a freedom and the other to a ground of discrimination. Regardless, I conclude that, where the conscience at issue is a religious conscience, as I have found Mr. Perren possessed, it is captured by the ground of religion and protected from discrimination.

[ 59 ] This interpretation aligns, in my view, with the Tribunal’s obligation to interpret the Act in a manner that advances its broad underlying policy considerations and quasi-constitutional status, as suggested by Justice Laforest in Robichaud v. Her Majesty the Queen as Represented by the Treasury Board , 1987 CanLII 73 (SCC) at para 8 and also to adopt a broad and expansive approach to religious freedom, which the Supreme Court of Canada warned “should not be prematurely narrowly construed”: Amselem at para 62.

The Respondent’s case law
[ 60 ] The Respondent points me to several cases from arbitration proceedings and other tribunals where the applicants attempted to make similar arguments as Mr. Perren to support an exemption to getting the COVID-19 vaccine:

A) God speaking to them through their conscience and telling them not to get vaccinated, amidst concerns that the vaccine can alter or instruct DNA, RNA or molecular structure ( Oulds v. Bluewater Health , 2023 HRTO 1134 [ Oulds ]);

B) Their personal convictions are directed by the true and living God; their body is the Temple of the Holy Spirit, and they must not defile it ; and citing concerns around the ingredients of the vaccination ( KK v. Hockey Northwestern Ontario , 2024 HRTO 725 [ KK ]);

C) They avoid taking medication or vaccines considered unsafe, ineffective or experimental, based on the available science, because they would not be at peace and once their mind is made up it becomes a sin to act against it ( Nova Scotia Union of Public & Private Employees, Local 13 v. Halifax Regional Municipality , 2022 CanLII 129860 (NS LA) [ NS UPPE, Local 13 ]); and

D) God would not want them to take something that would hurt them, citing concerns around the potential side effects or long-term adverse effects of the vaccine ( Corporation of the City of Vaughan v Canadian Union of Public Employees, Locals 905-20 (Hourly), 905-21 (F/t) And Local 905-22 (P/t) , 2024 CanLII 8991 (ON LA) [ Corporation of the City of Vaughan ] ).

[ 61 ] All of these arguments failed. The decision-makers in these cases took issue with the nexus between the applicants’ beliefs and religion (or creed in the case of the Human Rights Tribunal of Ontario (HRTO) jurisprudence).

[ 62 ] In Oulds , the HRTO found that the applicant’s creed lacked an “overarching systemic component” and that their belief appeared singular and focused on lack of efficacy, a perception of modifying DNA, and the need for autonomy in making this specific vaccine choice. The HRTO made a similar observation in K.K., noting an absence of nexus to any organization or community with a shared system of belief. It observed that the applicant’s particular belief appeared focused on their dislike of the ingredients of the COVID-19 vaccine and a perception that the vaccine was not safe.

[ 63 ] I n Corporation of the City of Vaughan , the grievor listed a series of concerns regarding the safety of the vaccine but provided no mention of her creed at the time of her termination. Although the evidence she subsequently submitted to the arbitrator mentioned her Catholic faith and her belief that God would not want her to take something that would hurt her, the arbitrator found that she established no nexus to a system of beliefs that are creed-based.

[ 64 ] Finally, in NS UPPE, Local 13 , the premise of the grievor’s belief appeared to originate from a scientific analysis of secular factors. As the arbitrator summarized it, “any personal decision she reaches regarding her health she considers to become protected as a religious belief”.

[ 65 ] The Respondent argues that bringing Mr. Perren’s objection to the COVID-19 vaccination within the realm of protected religious freedom would mean that he is entitled to protection for anything he feels uncomfortable doing on the basis that God would not want him to do that thing, irrespective of its connection to an underlying religious tenant. It relies on the arbitrator’s remarks in Corporation of the City of Vaughan at para 27:

The grievor’s belief is essentially a belief that God supports whatever actions she considers important and warranted. If this were sufficient to justify an exemption claim, then a grievor would be entitled to an exemption based on creed for everything a grievor was opposed to doing, since her God would not want her to do anything she was opposed to doing, provided she sincerely believed in her actions. Such a belief alone is not sufficient to entitle the grievor to an exemption. There must also be a connection or nexus with an overarching set of beliefs. A mere belief that God supports one’s actions is not sufficient.

[ 66 ] This argument is one which cautions me not to “open the flood gates”, so to speak, when it comes to recognizing religious beliefs. In addition to asking me to engage in a speculative exercise that goes beyond the facts of this case, the facts before me are not that Mr. Perren seeks to protect anything that he is uncomfortable with. Mr. Perren and his father explained that there were specific circumstances that give rise to the process of listening to their conscience and becoming convicted. The first was that Mr. Perren faced a challenge that required this reflection. In the case at hand, this involved a request from his employer that he become vaccinated as a condition of his employment, which came into tension with his religious belief that his body is a temple and that he needs to treat what goes into it with caution. The second was the process itself, which involved not only listening to the Holy Spirit but then testing his conscience before he could determine if he was convicted.

[ 67 ] The Respondent’s argument implies that the Evangelical faith, as understood and practiced by Mr. Perren, should not be interpreted to include the process of following one’s religious conscience as a protected religious belief. And yet this is the belief that Mr. Perren described, which his father shares and taught him, and which is grounded in their interpretation of scripture and faith as Evangelical Christians.

[ 68 ] I find that in calling on him to connect with God through fasting and prayer when faced with these circumstances and to heed to the conviction that emanates from this “personal connection with the divine”, his faith is calling for “a particular line of conduct” in line with the wording of the first stage of the Supreme Court’s two-part test at para 56 of Amselem . In my view, Mr. Perren, by all accounts, has met this threshold.

2. Mr. Perren was sincere
[ 69 ] The second part of the Amselem test is for the individual to show that he or she is sincere in his or her belief.

[ 70 ] I found Mr. Perren’s evidence, as supported by his father’s testimony, credible. Mr. Perren’s lifetime engagement with his faith, consistent reluctance to vaccinations, his and Reverand Perren’s consistent and coherent evidence describing the religious process by which they engage with God and which their faith protects, the scriptural interpretations that ground this belief, combined with Mr. Perren’s honest and forthright demeanour, convinced me of the sincerity of his belief that he was convicted by God not to receive the COVID-19 vaccine.

The timing of Mr. Perren’s conviction
[ 71 ] The Respondent argues that Mr. Perren’s and Reverand Perren’s evidence at the hearing indicates that Mr. Perren’s belief is not rooted in religion but rather is grounded in scientific and health-based concerns with the vaccine that pre-existed his stated conviction, particularly that the COVID-19 vaccination was a novel science. The Respondent relies, in support of this view, on the evidence that Mr. Perren presented where he indicated that he started to feel the Holy Spirit in the summer months of 2021. From December 2020, when the vaccines were first released, until he became convicted in the summer of 2021, Mr. Perren testified that he did not get the vaccine because he is cautious about what he puts in his body, which is a temple and the dwelling place of the Lord and, as he stated in cross-examination, “there was MRNA, potential for aborted fetal cells in there and as well the fact that it was novel as well”. The Respondent’s argument is that this evidence demonstrates that the reasons behind Mr. Perren’s refusal to get vaccinated were based on his discomfort with vaccination, borne of secular concerns. The timing of his conviction points to God supporting his decision not to be vaccinated, which is different from God requiring that he not be vaccinated.

[ 72 ] Mr. Perren explained the timing of his conviction by noting that prior to the summer of 2021, there was no urgency for him to get the vaccine and, therefore, no real thought behind it. He continued to live normally, which for him meant not getting vaccinated. He testified that, aside from vaccines he received as a baby, he has never taken any other vaccines. In other words, until pushed to determine whether his religious beliefs allowed him to take this particular vaccine, he operated as he always did.

[ 73 ] I agree with the Respondent that the concerns Mr. Perren held during this period were not religious. His fears that mRNA vaccines could alter his DNA are an example of this, and they did precede his conviction. I disagree, however, that these secular concerns signify that Mr. Perren’s objection to getting vaccinated was not based on a religious belief and that both his secular concerns and religious beliefs cannot coexist. Religion does not exist in separation from every day human life. Mr. Perren can possess secular fears regarding new vaccines, even some that are not borne out of scientific evidence and also hold a genuine conviction, through his relationship and consultation with the divine, that he has been told not to be vaccinated. Humans are complex creatures. They can hold both religious and non-religious beliefs on the same issue.

[ 74 ] In the end, the assessment I must make is one of sincerity. This evidence would only be relevant if it demonstrated that Mr. Perren’s reference to a religious belief was a pretext for what was truly a secular fear. I did not find this to be the case. I found Mr. Perren’s explanations of why he was only convicted in the summer of 2021 sincere and coherent with the rest of his evidence, including his past practices when it comes to taking vaccines. While Mr. Perren had some secular concerns, he only claimed to have become convicted once he had engaged in the process of listening to and testing his conscience and ascertaining what he perceived was God’s will for him.

Inconsistencies in Mr. Perren’s evidence
[ 75 ] The Respondent highlights that Mr. Perren’s evidence regarding his religious objection to the COVID-19 vaccine shifted during these proceedings and since his first communications with CN. In both his Request Form and his testimony in chief at the hearing, Mr. Perren discussed how he believed that he was being led by God, through the Holy Spirit and his conscience, not to get vaccinated. However, a month after his employer denied his request for an exemption to the vaccine mandate, Mr. Perren stated that he could not get “mRNA vaccinations due to his sincerely previously held religion” and that “the position of not taking Genetic Therapy or any Genetic Altering medical procedures is supported biblically”. In his complaint to the Tribunal, Mr. Perren states that he has “a very real, sincerely and previously held religious belief that I cannot be vaccinated with mNRA vaccines and/or any vaccine that uses fetal cells in the creation or testing of said vaccine”.

[ 76 ] Mr. Perren made no mention of DNA, genetic alteration, or fetal cells in his examination in chief. In response to my questions, he clarified that scripture states that the body is a temple and the residing place of the Holy Spirit and Jesus Christ and stated: “so you have to be careful with what you put in your body; if we are created in the image of God, which is what we believe, it goes down to DNA”. He testified that, as a result, he was cautious about what gets injected into his body “I don't want to put Tylenol or Advil or drugs, I’ll only put limited amount of things in body, I try to stay away from it”. In cross-examination, he stated that the potential of fetal cell use, mRNA technology, and the novelty of the vaccine were part of his concerns and objections to getting the vaccine before the summer of 2021, when he became convicted.

[ 77 ] The Respondent highlights that Mr. Perren never provided any explanation as to why fetal cell use would interfere with his religious belief or practice and argues that there was simply no clear, consistent, or otherwise credible evidence as to what religious belief or practice obligated Mr. Perren to not be vaccinated against COVID-19.

[ 78 ] I agree with the Respondent that Mr. Perren never clearly explained how the potential of fetal cell use related to his religious belief, nor did he expand on his concerns surrounding the mRNA technology beyond not knowing how it could impact his body or DNA. In the end, what I understood from Mr. Perren’s evidence was that these concerns were not, in and of themselves, what determined his belief that he could not be vaccinated. Rather, they were considerations that challenged his belief that his body is a temple, which, in turn, gave rise to the need for him to engage in his practice of consulting with God before being able to determine whether or not he could get vaccinated. I say could get vaccinated because Mr. Perren was clear and consistent that the decision not to get vaccinated was not a choice: “I don't chose, I get led, I get told to do so”.

[ 79 ] Even if I am wrong in my understanding of this portion of his evidence, I did not find that the lack of clarity surrounding these specific elements or the differences in his attempts to describe his belief at various points of this process undermined his credibility. Mr. Perren stated in his testimony that he often found it difficult to explain his religious beliefs and convictions with the verbiage that, while common within his religious community, is not as easy for someone who would not be familiar with certain terms to understand. It does not surprise me that he tried to reframe his belief when his first attempt appeared not to have been understood or believed by his employer. While the Respondent is correct that some of Mr. Perren’s testimony on these elements, such as his fear of mRNA technology and the novelty of the vaccine as well as concerns regarding genetic modifications, point to secular concerns, I found Mr. Perren’s testimony regarding the religious aspects of his belief to be credible and sincere. There can be several reasons for objecting to getting vaccinated. As long as one of them is sincerely and legitimately grounded in religion, as subjectively interpreted and applied, an individual is entitled to being accommodated: Public Health Sudbury & Districts v Ontario Nurses’ Association , 2022 CanLII 48440 (ON LA) at para 50.

B. Did the Complainant communicate his religious belief to the Respondent?
[ 80 ] The Respondent argues that if I find that Mr. Perren did provide credible evidence at the hearing that demonstrates that he had a sincere religious belief or practice which interfered with his ability to get vaccinated, what Mr. Perren provided to CN in his exemption request was insufficient to demonstrate that his sincerely held religious belief prevented him from being vaccinated.

[ 81 ] Mr. Perren took the following steps to obtain an accommodation from his employer:

A) On September 9, 2021, he emailed Ms. Hedley, Director of Human Resources, and asked how he could obtain a religious exemption from the vaccine mandate. Ms. Hedley responded that CN was still working through its process for these requests but asked Mr. Perren to provide details surrounding his faith. Mr. Perren wrote, “Sure, I am a bible believing Christian and have spent time in prayer about this and God has not afforded me a clear conscience in this matter. Not sure if this is what you were looking for, please let me know”.

B) On September 24, 2021, Valentina Carreiro, a member of the CN Human Resources and Labour Relations team and the administrative support for the Committee, instructed Mr. Perren to fill out the Request Form and return it to her. Mr. Perren sent her the completed form three days later. In response to the first question which asked him to “Please identify your sincerely held religious belief, practice, and/or observance that you believe conflicts with the Company's vaccination mandate”, Mr. Perren wrote, “I am a follower of Jesus and have spent many hours in prayer about this. After prayer, God has not afforded me a clear conscience with regards to taking this Vaccination. I must follow the path God leads me down as my faith is in him always”.

C) In response to the second question, “Please state how your particular sincerely held religious belief, practice, and/or observance specifically conflicts with the Company’s vaccination mandate, and describe the accommodation that you are requesting (also list any alternative accommodations that you believe will eliminate the conflict)”, Mr. Perren responded, “I must follow Jesus and without having a clear conscience about taking the vaccination I cannot take it. I am requesting an exemption from the vaccination mandate. I must follow God in all he asks of me. Yet my deep love and care for others make me determined to seek alternatives that ensure others safety. I will look to the Company for recommendations for alternatives that comply with their vaccination mandate”.

D) On October 8, 2021, Ms. Carreiro advised Mr. Perren that the Committee had carefully reviewed his submission and was denying his request for religious accommodation. She indicated that while his statement established that he was a “follower of Jesus”, it failed to establish that he had a “faith-based practice of belief that precludes vaccination”. In CN’s view, his choice not to get vaccinated was a personal one and was not a choice that it was required to accommodate. Mr. Perren responded and asked which religious leader CN had consulted when denying his request. He reiterated that his “faith-based practice is to consult with God ”. Ms. Carreiro responded on behalf of the Committee on October 12, 2021, and advised Mr. Perren that CN had reviewed the facts he had submitted surrounding his request for a religious exemption and had taken a final position that his request was not approved. Mr. Perren was therefore to comply with CN’s policy to be “fully vaccinated by November 1, 2021”.

E) On October 29, 2021, Mr. Perren wrote to Ms. Hedley, expressing confusion around the rejection of his religious exemption request. He noted that he had emails between him and his supervisor that preceded that vaccine mandate that relayed conversations they had regarding his religion and inability to be vaccinated. He added, “Can you help me understand what I need to do in order to keep my job beyond the 15th? Company has taken the position of being the expert on my religion but cannot tell me how or with whom was consulted to make the final decision. I find this disturbing. Thanks for your help”. Mr. Perren testified that Ms. Hedley responded that there was no process in place for him to grieve their decision and that this was the final decision.

F) On November 9, 2021, Jeff Bellerud, Mr. Perren’s manager, emailed a letter to Mr. Perren advising him that he needed to be vaccinated by November 15, 2021, barring which he would be placed on an unpaid leave. Mr. Perren testified that he called Mr. Bellerud and told him that he was in trouble and that CN was not willing to engage in a conversation. He told him that, given that he had such a deep conviction, he felt that CN was being discriminatory. Mr. Perren followed up with Mr. Bellerud by email, in which he stated that he could not get mRNA vaccinations “due to his sincerely previously held religion”. He added, “I grew up in Church as my Dad was a pastor and now holds the roll of District Superintendent of the Evangelical Free Church in the Pacific North West. The position of not taking Genetic Therapy or any Genetic Altering medical procedures is supported biblically, and my family and I are aligned with this as well. I would appreciate it if you would be able to get in contact with the religious exemption committee and have them contact me to discuss. I have emailed them with no success. I would like to discuss this with them and answer any questions they may have”. Mr. Bellerud did not testify at the hearing, but Ms. Lewis testified that she had never seen this email. The evidence before me suggests that this email was not forwarded to the Committee.

[ 82 ] Ms. Lewis explained the Respondent’s process for considering employee’s exemption requests to the vaccine mandate based on religious grounds. She testified that the members of the Committee would each read the employee’s submission and would meet to discuss the application and determine whether it met the criteria established in the Guidance Material. Pages 17 and 18 of the Guidance Material explain how the employer is to consider requests for accommodation on the ground of religion. It advises employers that the information provided by the requester must demonstrate that the belief is religious in nature, prevents full vaccination, and is sincerely held. In effect, the Guidance Material relays the Amselem test, which I have relied on in this case.

[ 83 ] Ms. Lewis testified that, in the case of Mr. Perren’s submission, the Committee did not doubt “the quality of his faith or religion” or his sincerity. However, it found that “Mr. Perren did not explain how his belief precluded him from being vaccinated”. While he had indicated that his conscience would not allow him to get vaccinated, the Committee found that he provided no additional indication of how this conflicted or was linked with his religion in a significant way. Ms. Lewis added,

not sure that conscience and religious belief are necessarily the same thing. The link just wasn't there. It didn't demonstrate how the vaccination would conflict with it, it was just, and I am paraphrasing, ‘my conscience won't allow me to take the vaccine’.

[ 84 ] Ms. Lewis indicated that CN did not ask Mr. Perren for further information or clarification because Mr. Perren’s response was clear. She testified that the Committee decided not to grant Mr. Perren the exemption because all of its members agreed that his objection to the vaccine was that he did not have a clear conscience, rather than a religious belief or practice. She noted that while the Committee accepted additional information sent in by employees when they did so of their own volition, there was no formal appeal process.

[ 85 ] Ms. Hedley testified that she recalled significant discussion among the Committee members regarding Mr. Perren’s request and the fact that there was an indication that his request reflected “more of a conscience decision more than a religious inhibitor”. When asked why the Committee did not request additional information from Mr. Perren, she responded that “it was clearly indicated that this was a conscious decision, not that this was based on religious sets of understanding or beliefs. In other applications we saw doctrines and scriptures and all sorts of other things. This was not about religion from our standpoint, this was a conscious decision”.

[ 86 ] I found both Ms. Lewis’ and Ms. Hedley’s statements that Mr. Perren’s submissions were “clear” that his request was not about religion to be inconsistent. Ms. Lewis highlighted the weakness in the Committee’s assumption that he was referring to a secular conscience when she expressed that she was “not sure” that conscience and religious belief were the same thing. In fact, as Mr. Perren’s evidence at the hearing explained, in his case they are the same thing.

[ 87 ] Ms. Hedley testified that Mr. Perren’s request was “more of” of a conscientious decision, suggesting that the Committee undertook a weighing exercise which dismissed any religious components of his request as secondary. However, even the wording of the Guidance Material that the Committee followed states that an exclusion based on religion does not apply to “beliefs, convictions or practices that are secular, socially based or only conscientiously held” (at 18). In other words, the Guidance Material left room for the possibility that individuals could possess religious and non-religious beliefs regarding vaccinations and limited eligibility for the exclusion to beliefs that are non-religious. Mr. Perren only needed to show that one of his beliefs preventing him from receiving the COVID-19 vaccine was a sincerely held religious belief for the Committee to grant him the exclusion (see Bombardier at paras 43–52).

[ 88 ] In the end, the Respondent took the position that it was Mr. Perren’s obligation to put his best foot forward. It argues that he understood the significance of his application and the importance of providing fulsome information in support of it and that nothing prevented him from providing additional information with his Request Form. The information he did provide, including his response to Ms. Carreira after receiving the denial, was also considered by the Committee. Ultimately, he failed to provide the Committee with enough evidence of the link between his belief and his religion.

[ 89 ] When we review the elements that Mr. Perren provided, I find that the Committee had sufficient information to know that it was in receipt of a request that could satisfy the threshold for a religious exemption. The Committee members knew that Mr. Perren:

· was a Bible-believing Christian and a follower of Jesus;

· had spent many hours in prayer regarding the COVID-19 vaccine;

· has a faith-based practice of consulting with God;

· was not afforded by God a clear conscience regarding the vaccine, and he must follow God’s will;

· must follow Jesus, and without having a clear conscience about taking the vaccine, he cannot take it;

· certified that the information he was providing was true and accurate when signing the Request Form;

· was willing to offer more information to the Committee if it needed it;

[ 90 ] Although never received by the Committee despite Mr. Perren’s request that it be forwarded to them, the Respondent also knew from Mr. Perren’s email to Jeff Bellerud that he had grown up in the church and that his father was a pastor of an Evangelical Free Church.

[ 91 ] Mr. Perren’s information revealed that he was a religious person, that he held a religious practice of praying to God, and that his conscience came from God. Having engaged in this practice, he indicated that it was God’s will for him not to get vaccinated, and he certified that this information was sincere. This information covered all three of the elements required in the Guidance Material and by Amselem . It is also what Mr. Perren and Reverand Perren explained in greater depth at the hearing.

[ 92 ] The issue was not that Mr. Perren did not understand the significance of his application or the importance of responding fully. He acknowledged that he was aware of this. The issue is that he genuinely did not know what the Committee did not understand from his application and what type of information it might need to be satisfied. The Committee could have asked for more information or evidence from Mr. Perren to satisfy itself that he met the Guidance Material criteria. It is common, in the context of a disability, for example, for an employer to ask an employee to provide evidence of their disability through medical records, doctors’ notes or other types of proof. Mr. Perren did repeatedly ask if the Committee required any additional information. He made multiple attempts to reach out to the members of the Committee and to other parts of his management team to try to understand its decision and clarify what it needed for him to be able to satisfy that he required accommodation.

[ 93 ] Instead, under the guise of being equitable to all employees, the Respondent adopted an approach that provided employees with only the information found on the exemption form and closed off any opportunity for a dialogue. Ms. Lewis and Ms. Hedley testified that this approach was based on them not wanting to “coach people around circumventing the regulation”. Ms. Lewis said:

The mandate of the committee was to evaluate the submissions that we received. It was not about providing instructions as to how to circumvent what we were told was government regulations on employees being vaccinated. We were very very careful to make sure that every employee had the same information because we were trying to be as equitable as we possibly could. Again, as I said with the ‘appeal’, it was a back and forth, with those who provided additional information we reviewed again. But as I said, it was not our mandate to coach people around circumventing the regulation. That is not what we were tasked with doing.

[ 94 ] Ms. Hedley used similar language during her testimony:

We didn’t provide guidance on how to avoid the mandate, we provided a process in which we would consider the information provided to us in terms of whether or not an exemption would be given. We did not provide direction on how to avoid getting the vaccination.

[ 95 ] And

The way that we approached the committee was that it was a requirement for the employee to disclose how the vaccination violated their religious beliefs, it was not for us to coach them on how to get the exemption.

[ 96 ] During cross-examination, Ms. Hedley appeared to correct this answer and admitted that Mr. Perren had not requested to circumvent the Ministerial Order. She aptly responded: “You made a request for accommodation”.

[ 97 ] This approach, which Mr. Perren described as a “police mentality”, is misaligned with what should have been the Committee’s objective: determining whether it had employees that required accommodation. More importantly, the problem with the Respondent’s process is that it leaves room for misunderstandings. As this case illustrates, the ground of religion is not always easy for an individual to explain and prove to those outside of his or her faith in a manner that they will understand or accept. While it is ultimately incumbent on an employee to establish the ground, this does not mean that they should be forced to play a guessing game of what their employer may or may not want or need to be fully satisfied.

[ 98 ] Once Mr. Perren provided the Committee with all of the elements of the test, it was incumbent on it to clarify with him anything that it did not understand. The evidence before me is that the Committee made an incorrect assumption in reviewing Mr. Perren’s application regarding the term “conscience” and based its decision on this assumption. I find that the responsibility for this incorrect assumption is entirely the Committee’s. Mr. Perren’s form referred to “God” affording him his conscience and linked following his conscience to following Jesus. Nothing about these responses suggested secularity. Rather than clarify its understanding, the Committee proceeded to make its determination and repeatedly decline the Complainant’s offer of further information and requests for guidance.

[ 99 ] I find, as a result, that the Committee has failed to disprove the Complainant’s prima facie case.

[ 100 ] The Respondent relies on Michalski v. McMaster University , 2022 ONSC 2625. In this case, the Ontario Superior Court found that the four students whose vaccine mandate exemption requests had been rejected by McMaster University had “an obligation to put their best foot forward”. The Court rejected the students’ arguments that the University should have provided them with the information the exemption review committee used in reviewing their requests, or should have requested specific information from them such as their prior practices regarding other vaccines and medications, or should have asked the students for additional information where their requests did not address factors under consideration. The Court found that the University’s process, including the exemption request form which explicitly instructed students to attach supporting documentation to substantiate their claim, was fair. It was incumbent upon the applicants, the Court concluded, to include all relevant information and documentation.

[ 101 ] I have not found this case helpful for a few reasons. The first is that the University characterized the applicants’ exemption requests as “political objections dressed up as religious argument” and rejected them because it concluded that they were using their sincerely held religious objection to abortion as a pretext for the real basis for their objection, which lied in personal and non-religious beliefs regarding the pandemic and the vaccines. These are not the facts of Mr. Perren’s case, whom I found to hold a sincere religious belief that prevented his vaccination.

[ 102 ] The second is that the Court undertakes its analysis of the fairness of the University’s process as part of an application for judicial review of administrative action. The Tribunal is not a reviewing court. Its jurisdiction is limited to findings of whether a discriminatory practice is substantiated pursuant to its statute. I am also not persuaded that adopting a procedural fairness standard from a process involving a University’s relationship with its students is appropriate in the context of employment, particularly since one of the factors considered was that the students, while significantly affected by the University’s decision, had no record of misconduct or discipline and their relationship with the University was not permanently severed (see Amselem at para 84). This is markedly different than the circumstances faced by Mr. Perren, whose eleven-year employment was terminated as a result of his refusal to get vaccinated.

[ 103 ] Finally, the Respondent asks me to view CN’s action in light of the context of the pandemic during which all of this unfolded. CN points to the fact that people were dying of the highly contagious Delta variant and that, at this point in time, the COVID-19 vaccine was recognized as being critical to saving lives. Exceptions to the vaccination requirements, CN argues, were “not to be lightly granted” and only those who “truly could not be vaccinated” were to be exempted.

[ 104 ] I agree that the pandemic context is important. Unfortunately, this is not the part of the analysis where it is most relevant. The Respondent’s case revolves around whether Mr. Perren did or did not have a religious belief. This analysis is centred on him, his religious belief, and the manner in which he sought to be accommodated. The test that Mr. Perren needed to meet was not that he “truly could not be vaccinated”. It was whether it was more likely than not that he had shown that he sincerely held a religious belief that he could not receive the vaccine. While there is nothing light about this onus, I am mindful not to let the context of the pandemic impose on individuals a higher standard of proof in establishing a prima facie case of discrimination.

[ 105 ] Arguments regarding the context of the pandemic could appropriately have been raised as part of CN’s defence. CN could have demonstrated, for example, that it could not accommodate the number of employees who were seeking medical and religious accommodations without undue hardship or that accommodating them in certain positions caused them undue hardship. CN did not raise any legal defences of this kind.

C. Did the Complainant experience an adverse impact?
[ 106 ] The second prong of the Moore framework requires me to determine whether Mr. Perren experienced an adverse impact. I prefer using the “adverse impact” standard in Moore over incorporating into the discrimination framework the “more than trivial or insubstantial interference” standard adopted in Amselem , which a claimant seeking a finding of a breach of the freedom of conscience and religion under the Charter must show. This is despite the fact that the “more than trivial or insubstantial interference” standard was referred to in the Guidance Material and adopted by the Respondent in its argument.

[ 107 ] The principal reason for my approach is that ultimately my analysis is one of equality, not of the expression of a freedom. Consequently, applying a test aimed at determining the breach of the freedom seems ill suited, even if they share a similar construct.

[ 108 ] Moreover, the Tribunal is a creature of statute and the Act is what guides my analysis. Section 7(b) defines a discriminatory practice in the course of employment as to directly or indirectly “differentiate adversely ” in relation to an employee on a prohibited ground of discrimination, language which is captured in the Moore framework.

[ 109 ] Finally, the Court’s explanation in Amselem of the meaning of the “more than trivial or insubstantial interference” standard reinforces this perspective. Over several paragraphs, the Court advises that the context of each case must be examined to ascertain whether the interference is more than trivial or insubstantial. This involves recognizing the broad and expansive approach to religious freedom while emphasizing that it has limits ( Amselem at paras 60–61). T his freedom does not allow individuals to do “absolutely anything in its name”, and individuals will still have to consider “how the exercise of their right impacts upon the rights of others in the context of the competing rights of private individuals”. Conduct which would potentially cause harm to or interference with the rights of others “would not automatically be protected” and “the ultimate protection of any particular Charter right must be measured in relation to other rights and with a view to the underlying context in which the apparent conflict arises”. Freedom of religion, like all other rights, “may be made subject to overriding societal concerns” ( Amselem at paras 62 and 63).

[ 110 ] In my view, this explanation suggests that the “more than trivial or insubstantial interference” standard under the Charter aims to address the need to balance freedom with other rights and concerns. Under the discrimination framework, this is what the Act largely aims to address as part of the section 15 defences and the determination of accommodation up to the point of undue hardship. This analysis occurs once the Tribunal finds that the complainant has already established a prima facie case for discrimination, which is an analysis that is centred on the experience of the complainant.

[ 111 ] In light of this, my adoption of the Amselem framework stops at the establishment of the ground of religion as part of the first prong of the Moore discrimination framework. I now proceed pursuant to the second prong of the prima facie test and look to determine the existence of an “adverse impact” .

[ 112 ] Has Mr. Perren experienced an adverse impact? The Federal Court of Appeal defined this notion as “something harmful, hurtful or hostile” ( Tahmourpour v. Canada (Attorney General) , 2010 FCA 192 at para 12 ), although the Tribunal has held that a fairly broad and permissive definition of “adverse” would still be consistent with the scheme of the Act: Kelsh v. Canadian Pacific Railway , 2019 CHRT 51 at para 112.

[ 113 ] The Respondent recognizes that Mr. Perren’s termination would constitute an adverse impact, and I agree. It adds, however, that despite his religious belief, Mr. Perren could still have received the COVID-19 vaccination and kept his employment without experiencing an adverse impact. This is because he took Tylenol when he deemed it necessary for pain relief despite not wanting to put it in his body and because Reverand Perren’s evidence was that foregoing one’s conscience on one occasion does not result in foregoing your religion since committing a sin is forgiven where forgiveness is genuinely sought through acknowledgment of one’s actions. In other words, even if Mr. Perren were to take the vaccine and commit a sin, he could repent and be forgiven.

[ 114 ] Given that Mr. Perren did not testify that he had been convicted not to take Tylenol, I am not persuaded by this part of the Respondent’s argument. I also find that were Mr. Perren to go against his conviction and get vaccinated, thereby committing a sin, this would constitute something harmful, despite the chance for forgiveness. Reverand Perren explained the consequences of going against one’s conscience.

You don’t lose your faith because you sin. The scripture doesn’t teach that we lose our salvation because we didn't do anything to merit salvation. There is nothing we can do. We were sinners before we were saved. The fact that we are sinners after we are saved doesn’t negate that. But I would have taught him that any fellowship he has with God is going to be seriously damaged if he knows he has done something and he doesn’t want to acknowledge that to God.

[ 115 ] Mr. Perren would undoubtedly experience an adverse impact if his employer required him to sin to keep his employment, even if he believes that he may be able to repair his fellowship with God afterwards.

D. Was the Complainant’s religion a factor in the adverse impact?
[ 116 ] It is undisputed that Mr. Perren was terminated because he did not receive the COVID-19 vaccine, contrary to the Ministerial Order. Given that I have determined that he made this decision because of a protected religious belief, I find that Mr. Perren has established the necessary causal link between the adverse impact and the ground of discrimination.

E. Was the Complainant harassed?
[ 117 ] On November 14, 2021, Mr. Perren was placed on unpaid leave, following which he received several letters regarding his projected date for termination:

A) On November 30, 2021, he received a letter advising him that he was not compliant with the Ministerial Order and that CN would terminate his employment on January 11, 2022, if he did not become vaccinated.

B) On January 10, 2022, he received a letter advising him that CN was maintaining his leave of absence because he was unvaccinated.

C) On January 26, 2022, he received a letter advising him that CN would be terminating his employment effective February 11, 2022, due to his unvaccinated status.

D) On January 27, 2022, he received a letter confirming that employees needed to be fully vaccinated in order to return to work.

E) On February 11, 2022, CN terminated his employment.

[ 118 ] Mr. Perren testified that he felt harassed by the Respondent’s constant threats that he should, as he put it, “get vaccinated, or else” despite him having repeatedly advised them of his sincerely held religious belief that was preventing him from doing so. He testified that the uncertainty around whether the Respondent would follow through on its threat of termination and at which date caused him severe anxiety, stress, and insomnia.

[ 119 ] Ms. Hedley explained that the letters that Mr. Perren received were template letters, sent to all employees who were in his position. CN’s objective was to provide employees with as much information as possible so that they could understand the evolving situation regarding the vaccine mandate, which CN had no control over.

[ 120 ] The Complainant did not raise section 14(c) of the Act in his complaint or his submissions, which is the provision that provides that it is a discriminatory practice to harass an individual on a prohibited ground of discrimination in matters related to employment. However, even if he had, I am not convinced that the events described meet the test for harassment, as articulated by Justice Tremblay-Lamer in Canada (HRC) v. Canada (Armed Forces) and Franke , 1999 CanLII 7907 (FC) at paras 29–50. While the conduct may have pertained to the prohibited ground of religion and a reasonable person may have known that receiving the letters would be unwelcome, I do not believe that they were of a nature that created a hostile or negative work environment. The process of putting an employee on unpaid leave and terminating their employment is inherently negative, and yet it occurs normally in workplaces. Although the Respondent was incorrect in its assessment that Mr. Perren did not possess a prohibited ground which should have exempted him from this process, I do not find that its approach towards him was out of the ordinary compared to its treatment of other employees and given the facts. At most, it reflects a confusing and stressful pandemic context which resulted in confusing and stressful directions to employees. I also have no evidence before me that Mr. Perren told his employer that he no longer wished to receive the letters or shared the level of stress and anxiety that they were producing. In the end, the stress and anxiety that he experienced appear to me to stem from the prospect of losing his employment, which originates from the discrimination because of his religion. It is more appropriately dealt with in the context of the remedies.

F. Did the Respondent breach the Charter?
[ 121 ] Neither party provided me with a significant argument regarding Mr. Perren’s allegation that the Respondent breached section 15 of the Charter in addition to the Act. The allegation, which featured only in his Statement of Particulars and was missing from his final submissions, was otherwise never elaborated upon. The Respondent briefly argued that the Tribunal lacks jurisdiction to entertain stand-alone Charter challenges and that Charter issues must arise in the Tribunal’s course of carrying out its statutory mandate to be appropriately dealt with. In its view, the appropriate application of the Charter in this case is the use of Charter principles as applied in the human rights context to determine whether Mr. Perren was discriminated against in his employment on the basis of religion.

[ 122 ] Without delving into the issue of jurisdiction, which is an important question here, I find that this is an argument that I can simply dispense with. Given my finding that the complaint is substantiated under the Act, there is no need for me to examine a parallel claim regarding a breach of section 15 of the Charter as well.

G. Remedies
[ 123 ] I have found that Mr. Perren’s complaint alleging discrimination by CN to be substantiated.
