Pursuant to section 53(2)(c) of the Act, where a complaint is found to be substantiated, the Tribunal can order that the person who engaged in the discriminatory practice compensate the victim for any or all of the wages that the victim was deprived of and for any expenses incurred by the victim as a result of the discriminatory practice. The purpose of this compensation is to place the complainant in the position they would have been in had the discrimination not occurred.

[ 124 ] In the present case, Mr. Perren seeks relief of lost wages, bonus, and severance payment in the amounts of $20,000.00, $14,400.59 and $25,000.00, respectively.

[ 125 ] Mr. Perren’s salary at CN was of $99,900 per year plus his bonus. After his termination, Mr. Perren worked for Bowline Logistics Ltd. as a long-haul truck driver from March 11 to July 4, 2022. According to the T4s he filed into evidence, he made $42,422.85 during this period. He began employment with Canadian Pacific Railway (CP) on July 28, 2022, making $35,356.71 in 2022. He subsequently earned a higher salary with CP than what he was making at CN, with a bonus and full benefits. While parties discussed the question of mitigation during the hearing, the Respondent did not argue that Mr. Perren failed to fully mitigate his losses in its final submissions. I find that Mr. Perren fulfilled this duty and showed an admirable ability to recover professionally from these difficult circumstances.

[ 126 ] The Respondent made no submissions on remedies in its final submissions. I conclude from its silence on the issue that it is not challenging Mr. Perren’s losses calculations. I am awarding Mr. Perren his lost wages in the amount of $20,000.00 and the $14,400.59 bonus, which he would have received had the discrimination not occurred. However, I find that I cannot also award him his severance payment as, had Mr. Perren not been terminated, he would not have received it. For me to award such a payment, in addition to the lost wages post-termination, would amount to a double recovery of damages, which I cannot legally grant: Hughes v. Canada (Attorney General), 2019 FC 1026 at para 46.

[ 127 ] In addition to lost wages, Mr. Perren also seek the sum of $20,000 under section 53(2)(e) of the Act for “injury to dignity, feelings and self-respect” and of $20,000 under section 53(3) of the Act for the Respondent’s discrimination in a willful and reckless manner.

[ 128 ] In determining what, if any, constitutes an appropriate award for pain and suffering in the circumstances, I must consider the objective seriousness of the conduct and the subjective impact that the discrimination had on Mr. Perren: Christoforou v. John Grant Haulage Ltd. , 2021 CHRT 15 at paras 104–105. Mr. Perren testified that these events caused him and his family tremendous stress and anxiety, something which he shared with his director, Mr. Bellerud. Prior to these events, he had taken medications for anxiety as well as insomnia but had been in the process of getting off them with his doctor. The anxiety he experienced when faced with the prospect of the termination, and the pressure he felt to get vaccinated despite having expressed that he could not do so given his relationship with Jesus, resulted in him having to take the medications again. He described it as a very chaotic time for him and his family.

[ 129 ] Accounting for the fact that the maximum award of $20,000 is reserved for the most serious cases ( Lafrenière v. Via Rail Canada Inc., 2019 CHRT 16 at para 193), I am awarding Mr. Perren $13,000.00 in pain and suffering. I find that the dismissive quality of CN’s response to his request for accommodation, combined with the seriousness of the termination of an eleven-year employment, are objective factors that support this award, as does the notable subjective impact that Mr. Perren described he experienced at the time of the events.

[ 130 ] As for Mr. Perren’s request for an award for willful and reckless behaviour under section 53(3) of the Act, I must make this determination in light of CN’s conduct and not on the effect that the conduct has had on Mr. Perren. As noted in Christoforou v. John Grant Haulage Ltd ., 2021 CHRT 15 at paras 106–111, a finding of willfulness requires an intention to discriminate and to infringe a person’s rights under the Act, whereas recklessness usually denotes acts that disregard or show indifference to the consequences, such that the conduct is done wantonly or needlessly. A finding of recklessness does not require proof of intention to discriminate.

[ 131 ] I have not found that CN exhibited any intention to discriminate. However, I do find that the Committee’s failure to clarify its understanding of Mr. Perren’s submission and repeated refusal to engage with him despite his attempts to understand its process and decision and to answer his questions regarding his religious belief exhibited a degree of recklessness that is not aligned with the spirit of accommodation that must exist in an employer-employee relationship and this warrants an award. I recognize that CN and the Committee were operating under extraordinary times, with short and shifting timelines, and that they were required to process dozens of these requests. In acknowledgement of these conditions, I am granting Mr. Perren $4,000.00 in special compensation.

[ 132 ] The Tribunal can make an award of interest on an order to pay compensation (section 53(4) of the Act) for a period that the member finds appropriate. Rule 46 of the Canadian Human Rights Tribunal Rules of Procedure, 2021 , SOR/2021-137 provides that interest awarded under section 53(4) must be simple interest that is equivalent to the bank rate established by the Bank of Canada and must accrue from the day on which the discriminatory practice occurred until the day on which the compensation is paid.

[ 133 ] I order an award of interest on all the compensation ordered in this case, which will accrue from the date of his suspension until it is paid.

VII. ORDER
[ 134 ] Within 30 days of this decision, CN is ordered to pay the following to Mr. Perren:

A) $20,000.00 in payment for lost wages (section 53(2)(c) of the Act);

B) $14,400.59 in payment for the lost bonus (section 53(2)(c) of the Act);

C) $13,000.00 in payment for pain and suffering (section 53(2)(e) of the Act); and

D) $4,000.00 in payment for special compensation (section 53(3) of the Act).

[ 135 ] Simple interest will accrue from November 17, 2021, on all payable compensation at a rate equivalent to the bank rate established by the Bank of Canada, calculated on a monthly basis .
